desc:
A cut point of a string s is a position between two neighbouring characters; a string of length n has n - 1 of them. Cutting at a point splits s into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part.

Return how many cut points produce two parts that are both palindromes.

For example, "aab" has one such cut point (aa|b), while "aaa" has two (a|aa and aa|a) and "abc" has none.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: There are only n - 1 cut points. For each one you just need to decide whether two pieces are palindromes.
A piece is a palindrome when it reads the same as its reverse. Compare s[:i] and s[i:] with their reversals.

Checking a piece costs O(n), so the total is O(n<sup>2</sup>), which is fine for n ≤ 3,000. This is exactly the first decision of a palindrome partition: the first piece must be a palindrome, and the rest must be partitionable too.
editorial: Try every cut point i from 1 to n - 1. The left part is s[:i] and the right part is s[i:]. A string is a palindrome when it equals its own reverse, so count the cut points where both parts pass this test.

Each test costs O(n) and there are n - 1 cut points, so the running time is O(n<sup>2</sup>) with O(n) extra memory for the slices. A linear solution exists (find all palindromic prefixes and suffixes with a prefix-function or Manacher pass), but it is not needed for these limits.

This tiny problem is the building block of palindrome partitioning: a partition is a sequence of cuts in which every piece is a palindrome, and the harder problems below ask you to count or list them.
